content: The following are professional interpretations of the provided references: 1. A study published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2017 (volume 65, pages 235-243) examined the clinical aspects of infectious diseases. 2. Jongbloed et al. conducted research on mortality among young Indigenous individuals who use drugs in British Columbia, as part of the Cedar Project. This study was published in CMAJ in 2017 (volume 189, pages E1352-E1359). 3. Benova et al. performed a systematic review and meta-analysis on the vertical transmission of the hepatitis C virus (HCV), published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2014 (volume 59, pages 765-773). 4. Jafari et al. explored the association between tattooing and the risk of HCV transmission through a systematic review and meta-analysis, published in the International Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2010 (volume 14, pages e928-e940). 5. Coppola et al. reviewed the prevalence of hepatitis B and C infections among healthcare workers, published in the World Journal of Hepatology in 2016 (volume 8, pages 273-281). 6. Westermann et al. conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on the prevalence of HCV among healthcare workers, published in Occupational and Environmental Medicine in 2015 (volume 72, pages 880-888). 7. Danta et al. investigated an epidemic of acute HCV in HIV-positive men who have sex with men, linked to high-risk sexual behaviors. This study was published in AIDS in 2007 (volume 21, pages 983-991). 8. Curry et al. evaluated the efficacy of sofosbuvir and velpatasvir in patients with decompensated cirrhosis due to HCV, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2015 (volume 373, pages 2618-2628). 9. Feld et al. assessed the effectiveness of sofosbuvir and velpatasvir in treating HCV genotypes 1, 2, 4, 5, and 6, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2015 (volume 373, pages 2599-2607). 10. Foster et al. studied the use of sofosbuvir and velpatasvir for HCV genotypes 2 and 3, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2015 (volume 373, pages 2608-2617). 11. Grebely et al. analyzed the safety and efficacy of sofosbuvir/velpatasvir in HCV patients undergoing opioid substitution therapy, based on phase 3 ASTRAL trials, published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2016 (volume 63, pages 1479-1481). 12. Wyles et al. conducted an open-label phase 3 study on the use of sofosbuvir and velpatasvir in patients co-infected with HCV and HIV-1, published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2017 (volume 65, pages 6-12). 13. Kateera et al. evaluated the safety and efficacy of sofosbuvir-velpatasvir in treatment-naïve HCV patients in Rwanda as part of the SHARED-3 trial, published in The Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology in 2022. 14. Asselah et al. examined the efficacy of glecaprevir/pibrentasvir for 8 or 12 weeks in patients with HCV genotypes 2, 4, 5, or 6 without cirrhosis, published in Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology in 2018 (volume 16, pages 417-426). 15. Forns et al. conducted a phase 3 trial (EXPEDITION-1) on glecaprevir/pibrentasvir in adults with HCV genotypes 1, 2, 4, 5, or 6 and compensated cirrhosis, published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2017 (volume 17, pages 1062-1068). 16. Gane et al. studied the use of glecaprevir and pibrentasvir in HCV patients with severe renal impairment, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2017 (volume 377, pages 1448-1455). 17. Gane et al. also evaluated the efficacy of ABT-493 and ABT-530 in HCV patients with genotypes 1 or 3 and compensated cirrhosis, published in Gastroenterology. 18. Kwo et al. demonstrated high response rates with glecaprevir and pibrentasvir in HCV patients with genotypes 1-6 without cirrhosis, published in Journal of Hepatology in 2017 (volume 67, pages 263-271). 19. Poordad et al. assessed the use of glecaprevir and pibrentasvir for 12 weeks in HCV genotype 1 patients with prior direct-acting antiviral treatment, published in Hepatology in 2017 (volume 66, pages 389-397). 20. Rockstroh et al. presented findings on the efficacy and safety of glecaprevir/pibrentasvir in HCV and HIV-1 co-infected patients as part of the EXPEDITION-2 study. 21. Antonini et al. reported on sofosbuvir-based regimens in HIV/HCV co-infected patients post-liver transplantation, based on the ANRS CO23 CUPILT study, published in Transplantation in 2018 (volume 102, pages 119-126). 22. Lacombe et al. evaluated the real-world efficacy of daclatasvir and sofosbuvir, with or without ribavirin, in HIV/HCV co-infected patients with advanced liver disease, published in Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2017 (volume 75, pages 97-107). 23. Lionetti et al. demonstrated the safety and efficacy of sofosbuvir plus daclatasvir, with or without ribavirin, for post-transplant HCV recurrence and severe fibrosis or cirrhosis, published in Clinical Transplantation in 2018. 24. Gupta et al. conducted a single-arm trial (SHARED) on the treatment of chronic HCV in Rwanda using ledipasvir-sofosbuvir, published in The Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology in 2019 (volume 4, pages 119-126). 25. The World Health Organization (WHO) released a global progress report in 2020 on overcoming barriers to HCV diagnostics and treatment in lowand middle-income countries. 26. The WHO also published a handbook for guideline development (2nd edition), accessed in March 2022. 27. Guyatt et al. developed GRADE guidelines for rating the quality of evidence, addressing imprecision, indirectness, inconsistency, publication bias, and study limitations, published in Journal of Clinical Epidemiology in 2011. 28. The HCV market intelligence report (2021) provided insights into market trends and challenges in HCV treatment. 29. Gopalakrishna et al. applied the GRADE framework to diagnostic tests, highlighting its challenges and feasibility, published in Journal of Clinical Epidemiology in 2014 (volume 67, pages 760-768). 30. Schünemann et al. discussed grading the quality of evidence and strength of recommendations for diagnostic tests and strategies, published in BMJ in 2008 (volume 336, pages 1106-1110). 31. Andrews et al. outlined the significance and presentation of recommendations in GRADE guidelines, published in Journal of Clinical Epidemiology in 2013 (volume 66, pages 719-725). 32. Whiting et al. introduced QUADAS-2, a revised tool for assessing the quality of diagnostic accuracy studies, published in Annals of Internal Medicine in 2011 (volume 155, pages 529-536). 33. Indolfi et al. reviewed HCV infection in children and adolescents, published in The Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology in 2019 (volume 4, pages 477-487). 34. Malik et al. conducted a global review of national HCV policies for children, published in JHEP Reports in 2021 (volume 3, article 100227). 35. Schmelzer et al. modeled the global prevalence of HCV in children in 2018, published in The Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology in 2020 (volume 5, pages 374-392). 36. Indolfi et al. provided a position paper on treating chronic HCV in children, published in Journal of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Nutrition in 2018 (volume 66, pages 505-515). 37. Modin et al. reviewed the epidemiology and natural history of HCV in children and young people, published in Journal of Hepatology in 2019 (volume 70, pages 371-378). 38. Serranti et al. evaluated an 8-week course of sofosbuvir/ledipasvir therapy in adolescents with chronic HCV, published in Journal of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Nutrition in 2019 (volume 69, pages 595-598). 39. Murray et al. assessed the safety and efficacy of ledipasvir-sofosbuvir in children aged 6-11 years with chronic HCV, published in Hepatology in 2018 (volume 68, pages 2158-2166). 40. Rosenthal et al. studied sofosbuvir and ribavirin therapy in children aged 3 to <12 years with HCV genotypes 2 or 3, published in Hepatology in 2020 (volume 71, pages 31-43). 41. Mack et al. provided NASPGHAN practice guidelines for diagnosing and managing HCV in infants, children, and adolescents, published in Journal of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Nutrition in 2012 (volume 54, pages 838-855). 42. Druyts et al. conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on the efficacy and safety of pegylated interferon alfa-2a or alfa-2b plus ribavirin in children with chronic HCV, published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2013 (volume 56, pages 961-967). 43. Wirth et al. reported on peginterferon alfa-2b plus ribavirin treatment in children with chronic HCV, published in Hepatology in 2005 (volume 41, pages 1013-1018). 44. Jara et al. evaluated the efficacy and safety of peginterferon-alpha 2b and ribavirin combination therapy in children with chronic HCV, published in Pediatric Infectious Disease Journal in 2008 (volume 27, pages 142-148). 45. Sokal et al. studied peginterferon alfa-2a plus ribavirin for chronic HCV in children and adolescents, published in Journal of Hepatology in 2010 (volume 52, pages 827-831). 46. Tajiri et al. surveyed the use of peginterferon alpha-2b and ribavirin in Japanese pediatric and young adult patients with chronic HCV, published in European Journal of Gastroenterology & Hepatology in 2009 (volume 21, pages 1256-1260). 47. Baker et al. examined the response to pegylated interferon alpha-2b and ribavirin in children with chronic HCV, published in Journal of Clinical Gastroenterology in 2007 (volume 41, pages 111-114). 48. Indolfi et al. analyzed the kinetics of virologic response to pegylated interferon and ribavirin in children with chronic HCV, published in Pediatric Infectious Disease Journal in 2016 (volume 35, pages 1300-1303). 49. Balistreri et al. assessed the safety and effectiveness of ledipasvir-sofosbuvir in adolescents aged 12-17 years with HCV genotype 1, published in Hepatology in 2017 (volume 66, pages 371-378). 50. Wirth et al. evaluated sofosbuvir and ribavirin in adolescents aged 12-17 years with HCV genotypes 2 or 3, published in Hepatology in 2017 (volume 66, pages 1102-1110). 51. Garrison et al. studied the pharmacokinetics of once-daily sofosbuvir and ledipasvir/sofosbuvir in HCV-infected children aged 6 to <12 years, published in 2016. 52. Yakoot et al. evaluated dual sofosbuvir/daclatasvir therapy in adolescent patients with chronic HCV, published in Journal of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Nutrition in 2018 (volume 67, pages 86-89). 53. Abdel Ghaffar et al. assessed the safety and efficacy of combined sofosbuvir/daclatasvir treatment in children and adolescents with HCV genotype 4, published in Journal of Viral Hepatitis in 2019 (volume 26, pages 263-270). 54. Jonas et al. reported on the pharmacokinetics, safety, and efficacy of glecaprevir/pibrentasvir in adolescents with chronic HCV as part of the DORA study, published in Hepatology in 2020 (volume 71, pages 456-462). 55. Jonas et al. also studied glecaprevir/pibrentasvir in children with chronic HCV as part of the DORA study, published in Hepatology in 2021 (volume 74, pages 19-27). 56. Hirsch et al. shared a Brazilian single-center experience with direct-acting antivirals for children with chronic HCV, presented at the ESPID Meeting in 2020. 57. Rodrigue et al. examined the impact of HCV infection on children and their caregivers, focusing on quality of life, cognitive, and emotional outcomes, published in Journal of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Nutrition in 2009 (volume 48, pages 341-347). 58. Nydegger et al. studied health-related quality of life in children with HCV acquired in the first year of life, published in Journal of Gastroenterology & Hepatology in 2008 (volume 23, pages 226-230). 59. Younossi et al. evaluated health-related quality of life in adolescent patients with HCV genotype 1 treated with sofosbuvir and ledipasvir, published in Journal of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Nutrition in 2018 (volume 66, pages 112-116). 60. Younossi et al. also assessed quality of life in adolescents with HCV treated with sofosbuvir and ribavirin, published in Journal of Viral Hepatitis in 2018 (volume 25, pages 354-362). 61. The FDA provided guidance for developing direct-acting antiviral drugs for chronic HCV treatment. 62. Al-Nahari et al. studied the pharmacokinetics of daclatasvir in Egyptian adolescents with HCV genotype 4, published in Antiviral Therapy in 2020 (volume 25, pages 101-110). 63. Chan et al. conducted a population pharmacokinetic analysis of daclatasvir in subjects with chronic HCV, published in Clinical Pharmacokinetics in 2017 (volume 56, pages 1173-1183). 64. Cressey et al. 65. Rosenthal et al. demonstrated the safety and efficacy of sofosbuvir + ribavirin for 12 or 24 weeks in children aged 3 to <12 years with HCV genotypes 2 or 3. 66. Begley et al. studied the pharmacokinetics of once-daily sofosbuvir or ledipasvir/sofosbuvir in HCV-infected children aged 3 to <6 years, published in Hepatology in 2018. 67. Haber et al. reported on the long-term follow-up of children treated with peginterferon and ribavirin for HCV, published in Journal of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Nutrition in 2017 (volume 64, pages 89-94). 68. Molleson et al. investigated the development of autoantibodies and autoimmune disease during HCV treatment in children, published in Journal of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Nutrition in 2013 (volume 56, pages 304-310). 69. Narkewicz et al. studied ophthalmologic complications in children with chronic HCV treated with pegylated interferon, published in Journal of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Nutrition in 2010 (volume 51, pages 183-186). 70. Zheng et al. reported a case of fulminant type 1 diabetes caused by peginterferon-2a therapy in HCV, published in Journal of Diabetes in 2018 (volume 10, pages 419-420). 71. Walzer and Flamm reviewed emerging data on pegylated IFN-alpha and ribavirin in special populations, published in Expert Review of Clinical Pharmacology in 2009 (volume 2, pages 67-76). 72. Bortolotti et al. examined the long-term course of chronic HCV in children, from viral clearance to end-stage liver disease, published in Gastroenterology in 2008 (volume 134, pages 1900-1907). 73. Badizadegan et al. described the histopathology of the liver in children with chronic HCV, published in 1998 (volume 28, pages 1416-1423). 74. The European Medicines Agency provided personal communication on HCV treatment in children in 2019. 75. El-Sayed and Indolfi discussed the challenges of HCV treatment in children for HCV elimination, published in Seminars in Liver Disease in 2020 (volume 40, pages 213-224). 76. Kamal et al. reported on nationwide HCV screening and treatment of adolescents in Egyptian schools, published in The Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology in 2022. 77. The WHO released the 22nd model list of essential medicines in 2021. 78. The WHO also published global standards for quality healthcare services for adolescents, accessed in March 2022. 79. WHO guidance for HIV testing and care for adolescents living with HIV was also accessed in March 2022. 80. Elsharkawy et al. shared lessons from Egypt on prioritizing direct-acting antivirals for HCV treatment in resource-limited settings, published in Journal of Hepatology in 2018 (volume 68, pages 691-698). 81. The Global Hepatitis Report (2017) provided insights into the global burden of hepatitis. 82. Ford et al. outlined ten priorities for expanding HCV treatment access for people who inject drugs in lowand middle-income countries, published in International Journal of Drug Policy in 2015 (volume 26, pages 1088-1093). 83. Ishizaki et al. surveyed programmatic experiences and challenges in delivering hepatitis B and C testing in lowand middle-income countries, published in BMC Infectious Diseases in 2017 (volume 17, article 696). 84. Feld discussed the simplification of HCV diagnostics, published in Clinical Liver Disease (Hoboken) in 2018 (volume 12, pages 125-129). 85. Patel et al. reviewed innovations in HCV screening and treatment, published in Hepatology Communications in 2021 (volume 5, pages 371-386). 86. Grebely et al. explored the potential for single-visit HCV diagnosis using point-of-care diagnostics, published in Expert Review of Molecular Diagnostics in 2017 (volume 17, pages 1109-1115). 87. Kredo et al. reviewed task-shifting from doctors to non-doctors for initiating and maintaining antiretroviral therapy, published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in 2014. 88. Suthar et al. examined the integration and decentralization of antiretroviral therapy services to improve scale-up and effectiveness, published in AIDS in 2014 (volume 28, supplement 2, pages S175-S185). 89. Dolan et al. assessed the global burden of HIV, viral hepatitis, and tuberculosis in prisoners and detainees, published in The Lancet in 2016 (volume 388, pages 1089-1102). 90. The Global State of Harm Reduction (2016) report provided insights into harm reduction strategies. 91. Hellard et al. studied the prevalence and risk behaviors associated with HCV transmission in Australian correctional facilities, published in Epidemiology and Infection in 2004 (volume 132, pages 409-415). 92. Larney et al. conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on the incidence and prevalence of HCV in prisons and other closed settings, published in Hepatology in 2013 (volume 58, pages 1215-1224). 93. Bajis et al. reviewed interventions to enhance HCV testing, linkage to care, and treatment uptake among people who inject drugs, published in International Journal of Drug Policy in 2017 (volume 47, pages 34-46). 94. Jones et al. evaluated the effectiveness of interventions to increase HCV testing uptake among high-risk groups, published in European Journal of Public Health in 2013 (volume 24, pages 781-788). 95. Lazarus et al. reviewed HCV treatment uptake among people who inject drugs in the European region, published in BMC Infectious Diseases in 2014 (volume 14, supplement 6, article S16). 96. Mathes et al. identified factors influencing adherence in HCV-infected patients, published in BMC Infectious Diseases in 2014 (volume 14, article 203). 97. McDermott et al. reviewed outpatient directly observed therapy for HCV among people who use drugs, published in Journal of Virus Eradication in 2018 (volume 4, pages 118-122). 98. Tucker et al. conducted a qualitative meta-synthesis and systematic review of studies to improve linkage to care, adherence, and retention in public health HIV interventions, published in EBioMedicine in 2017 (volume 17, pages 163-171). 99. Wade et al. reviewed community-based HCV treatment, published in BMC Infectious Diseases in 2016 (volume 16, article 202). 100. Zhou et al. reviewed interventions to optimize the care continuum for chronic viral hepatitis, published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2016 (volume 16, pages 1409-1422). 101. Oru et al. reviewed decentralization, integration, and task-shifting in HCV testing and treatment, published in The Lancet Global Health in 2021 (volume 9, pages e431-e445). 102. Fairall et al. conducted a pragmatic, parallel, cluster-randomized trial on task-shifting antiretroviral therapy from doctors to primary-care nurses in South Africa (STRETCH), published in The Lancet in 2012 (volume 380, pages 889-898). 103. Seidman and Atun reviewed the cost savings and efficiency of task-shifting for health systems in lowand middle-income countries, published in Human Resources for Health in 2017 (volume 15, article 29). 104. Sharma et al. conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of communityand facility-based HIV testing to address linkage-to-care gaps in sub-Saharan Africa, published in Nature in 2015 (volume 528, pages S77-S85).
